title: Government & Democracy · Episode 3
chapters: Human rights: where they come from
The Geneva Conventions: rules for the worst of times

units.t: Government & Democracy. Episode three.
In this episode: Human rights: where they come from, The Geneva Conventions: rules for the worst of times and The United Nations.
Part one. Human rights: where they come from.
In 1948, after the horrors of the Second World War, the world's nations agreed on a list of rights belonging to every person.
Here's what's in it, and how Australia protects rights without a bill of rights.
Rights for every person.
Human rights are the basic freedoms that belong to every person, regardless of nationality, sex, race or religion.
The idea has deep roots.
Magna Carta limited a king's power in 1215, Enlightenment thinkers wrote of natural rights, and France in 1789 and the United States in 1791 put rights into law.
But the idea that rights apply to all humanity, as an international concern, took shape after 1945.
A UN commission chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt drafted a common standard.
Australia sat on the eight-country drafting committee, and H.
V.
Evatt was President of the General Assembly when the Universal Declaration was adopted in Paris on 10 December 1948, by 48 votes to none with eight abstentions.
Its first article: 'All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.'
From declaration to treaties.
The Universal Declaration was not a treaty, so it didn't directly bind countries in law.
It was a statement of shared aims, though it has become enormously influential and has shaped many constitutions and laws.

To turn its principles into binding obligations, the UN adopted two major treaties in 1966: the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights.
Together with the Declaration, they are often called the International Bill of Human Rights.
Other treaties followed on specific issues, including racial discrimination, discrimination against women, torture, children's rights and disability.
Two kinds of rights.
Civil and political rights mainly protect people from the misuse of state power and guarantee participation in public life.
They include the right to life, a fair trial, freedom of expression, religion and assembly, privacy, and the right to vote.
Many can be limited in certain circumstances, for example to protect public safety or the rights of others, but some, such as the ban on torture, are treated as absolute.
Economic, social and cultural rights cover fair work, joining a union, social security, adequate food and housing, health and education.
Because these depend on resources, countries must achieve them progressively.
Some argue they are as fundamental as civil rights, since freedom means little without food or schooling.
Others see them as policy goals for elected governments rather than rights for courts to enforce.
Australia's approach.
Australia is often described as the only Western democracy without a national bill or charter of rights.
Instead, rights are protected in several ways.
The Constitution contains a few express rights and an implied freedom of political communication.
The common law presumes Parliament doesn't intend to override basic freedoms unless it says so clearly.
Federal laws ban discrimination on grounds including race, 1975, sex, 1984, disability, 1992, and age, 2004, and the Australian Human Rights Commission handles complaints.
Since 2012, new federal bills must carry a statement on their compatibility with human rights, reviewed by a parliamentary committee.
The ACT, Victoria and Queensland have their own human rights Acts.
The debate, and your rights.
Supporters of a national bill of rights say current protections have gaps, that ordinary laws can be changed by any Parliament, and that a clear list would help vulnerable people.
Critics say elected Parliaments, not unelected judges, should balance rights, and that Australia already protects rights well.
A middle path is the Victorian model, where courts can declare laws inconsistent with rights but Parliament has the final say.
If you face discrimination at work, in housing, in education or from services, you can complain to the Australian Human Rights Commission or a state body.
In 1994, in Toonen v Australia, the UN Human Rights Committee found Tasmania's laws criminalising homosexual acts breached the right to privacy, and federal law changed soon after.
For advice on your situation, see a lawyer or community legal centre.
The key idea: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted on 10 December 1948, set out rights that belong to every person simply because they are human.
Part two. The Geneva Conventions: rules for the worst of times.
Even war has laws.
They began with a Swiss businessman who stumbled onto a battlefield and could not forget what he saw.
From Solferino to Geneva.
In June 1859, Swiss businessman Henry Dunant travelled to northern Italy hoping to meet Napoleon III about a business venture.
He arrived just after the Battle of Solferino.
Tens of thousands lay dead or wounded, with little medical help.
Dunant organised local villagers, many of them women, to care for the wounded of both sides.
His 1862 book, A Memory of Solferino, proposed trained volunteer relief groups and an international agreement protecting the wounded and their carers.
In 1863 he and four other Genevans formed the committee that became the International Committee of the Red Cross.
In 1864 twelve states signed the first Geneva Convention.
Wounded and sick soldiers had to be cared for on either side, and ambulances, hospitals and medical staff were protected, marked by a red cross on white, the reverse of the Swiss flag.
A late honour.
Dunant's own story did not end happily for many years.
His business ventures in Algeria failed, he went bankrupt in the 1860s, and the scandal forced him out of the organisation he had helped create.
He drifted through Europe in poverty and eventually settled in the small Swiss town of Heiden, where he lived quietly in a hospital home.
In the 1890s a journalist rediscovered him, and his story spread again.
In 1901 Dunant shared the very first Nobel Peace Prize with the French peace campaigner Frédéric Passy.
He died in 1910.
His birthday, 8 May, is now celebrated as World Red Cross and Red Crescent Day.
Four conventions.
The original treaty was updated in 1906 and 1929, but the Second World War exposed its limits.
Millions of prisoners of war died in captivity, and civilians suffered mass killings, deportations and starvation under occupation.
In 1949 states agreed on four new Geneva Conventions.
The first protects wounded and sick soldiers on land.
The second does the same for those wounded, sick or shipwrecked at sea.
The third sets out how prisoners of war must be treated, including humane conditions and protection from torture and public curiosity.
The fourth, entirely new, protects civilians in enemy hands and in occupied territory.
Every country in the world has ratified the 1949 conventions, which makes them truly universal.
The key principles.
Two Additional Protocols in 1977 strengthened protections for civilians and for victims of civil wars.
Together with other treaties, such as the Hague Conventions on weapons and tactics, they form international humanitarian law.
A few principles run through it.
Distinction means combatants must tell military targets from civilians, and may only target the former.
Proportionality means an attack is unlawful if the expected harm to civilians would be excessive compared with the concrete military advantage.
People who are no longer fighting, such as the wounded, the sick and those who surrender, must be treated humanely.
These rules do not decide whether a war is justified.
They apply equally to all sides, whatever the cause.
Emblems and enforcement.
The red cross emblem is protected by law and must not be misused, even for decoration or advertising.
The red crescent has been used since the 1870s, and in 2005 states adopted a third emblem, the red crystal, with no religious or national associations.
Enforcement is the hardest part.
The conventions require states to search for and prosecute people accused of grave breaches, such as wilful killing, torture or taking hostages, whatever their nationality.
Australia does this through its own legislation, including the Geneva Conventions Act 1957.
Since the 1990s, international tribunals and the International Criminal Court have also tried war crimes.
Violations still happen far too often, but the rules give victims a standard and the world a way to judge.
The key idea: One businessman's horror at a battlefield led to the Red Cross and the first Geneva Convention.
Part three. The United Nations.
Born from the ashes of the Second World War, the UN has 193 members, a veto that can freeze it, and agencies that helped wipe out smallpox.
Here's how it works and why it divides opinion.
Founded in 1945.
The United Nations was created as the Second World War ended, to prevent another global war.
Its predecessor, the League of Nations, founded in 1920, had failed to stop aggression in the 1930s, partly because major powers were absent or left.
Delegates from 50 countries signed the UN Charter in San Francisco on 26 June 1945, and Poland soon became the 51st founding member.
The Charter came into force on 24 October 1945, now marked as United Nations Day.
Australia was a founding member, and its delegation, led by H.
V.
Evatt, pushed for a stronger voice for smaller and middle powers.
Membership has grown to 193 countries, with headquarters in New York.
The Assembly and other organs.

The Charter created six principal organs: the General Assembly, the Security Council, the Economic and Social Council, the International Court of Justice in The Hague, the Secretariat, and the Trusteeship Council, suspended in 1994 after its last territory, Palau, became independent.
The Secretariat is the UN's staff, led by the Secretary-General, who serves a five-year term.
The General Assembly is the most representative body.
All 193 members sit in it, with one vote each, whether China or tiny Tuvalu.
It meets from September in New York, debates global issues, approves the budget and elects the Council's non-permanent members.
Important questions need a two-thirds majority.
But most of its resolutions are recommendations, not binding law, so they carry moral and political weight rather than legal force.
The Security Council veto.
The Security Council is the UN's most powerful body.
It has 15 members: five permanent members, China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States, and ten elected for two-year terms.
Its decisions on threats to peace can be binding on all members, and it can impose sanctions or authorise military force.
Each permanent member has a veto: a single 'no' vote blocks any substantive resolution.
The veto was the price of getting the great powers to join.
It has been used many times, most often by the Soviet Union or Russia and by the United States, and has often left the Council deadlocked.
At San Francisco, Australia argued against the full scope of the veto, without success.
Agencies and peacekeepers.
Much of the UN's work happens through agencies.
The World Health Organization coordinated the campaign that eradicated smallpox, declared in 1980.
UNICEF supports children's health, nutrition and education.
UNHCR protects people forced from their homes.
The World Food Programme, which won the 2020 Nobel Peace Prize, delivers food aid in crises.
UNESCO runs the World Heritage list, which includes the Great Barrier Reef, Uluru-Kata Tjuta and the Sydney Opera House.
Peacekeeping isn't mentioned in the Charter; it developed through practice.
Australians were among the first UN military observers, in Indonesia in 1947.
Peacekeepers, the 'blue helmets', are troops and police lent by member states to monitor ceasefires and protect civilians.
There have been successes, but also grave failures, notably Rwanda in 1994 and Srebrenica in 1995.
Strengths and criticisms.
Supporters argue the UN has helped avoid a third world war, given every nation a voice, delivered aid to millions, and set shared standards from human rights to aviation.
It gives rivals a place to keep talking.

Critics say the veto lets any permanent member block action even during atrocities, that the Council reflects the power of 1945 rather than today, that the organisation can be slow and bureaucratic, and that one-country-one-vote gives tiny and huge nations equal weight.
Reform is hard because changing the Charter needs the permanent members' agreement.
Australia held the Council's first presidency in 1946 and has served several terms as an elected member.
Tens of thousands of Australian personnel have served in UN and UN-authorised missions, including Cyprus, Cambodia and East Timor.
The key idea: The UN was founded in 1945 to prevent another world war after the League of Nations failed, and now has 193 members.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What idea lies at the heart of the 1948 Universal Declaration?
Answer. Rights belong to every person simply because they are human.
Question two. What did the first Geneva Convention require?
Answer. Wounded and sick soldiers to be cared for on either side.
Question three. Why was the UN created at the end of the Second World War?
Answer. To prevent another global war after the League failed.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
